abstract: Ancient whole-genome duplications (WGDs) have shaped flowering plant evolution, but their placement is sometimes uncertain, especially in clades primarily studied through transcriptomes. In such datasets, peaks in synonymous substitutions among paralogs (Ks) and phylogenomic gene-duplication mapping can identify large-scale gene family expansions (GFEs), but these approaches may disagree and, on their own, cannot distinguish WGD from chromosomal duplication or other genome-scale duplication mechanisms. These discrepancies may stem from biological processes such as diploidization, hybridization, and incomplete lineage sorting, or from systematic biases introduced by hidden gene paralogy that current pipelines fail to address. Here, we present H2O (homolog-to-ortholog), a workflow that integrates Ks distributions with tree-based conservative gene duplication calls (node-partitioned Ks distributions) and orthology inference with duplication-informed data-filtering methods. It improves the detection and placement of transcriptome-inferred GFEs while reducing errors from hidden paralogy. We evaluated H2O using simulated datasets and three empirical datasets (Ericales and two Caryophyllales subclades), refining large-scale GFE placements and comparing phylogenomic outcomes with those of ASTRAL-Pro and Yang and Smith (2014). Across empirical datasets, node-partitioned Ks distributions improved confidence in large-scale GFE placement and, under conservative phylogenetic data filtering, significantly reduced associated gene tree discordance. Reduced discordance comes at the cost of substantial data removal. Through simulation, we demonstrated that H2O's data-filtering methods effectively removed all paralogous relationships that orthology inference methods sometimes report, reducing gene tree discordance. These results highlight the need to treat transcriptome-inferred GFEs cautiously, integrate multiple lines of evidence, and explicitly account for hidden paralogy in plant phylogenomics.
